title: The first time most people hear about the giants before the Flood, they either laugh… or become deeply unsettled.
paragraphs: The first time most people hear about the giants before the Flood, they either laugh… or become deeply unsettled.
Because something inside the human soul recognizes this story feels forbidden.
Half-whispered through broken civilizations, scattered myths, hidden ruins, corrupted bloodlines, and terrifying biblical warnings most modern churches barely touch anymore.
But the Bible does not avoid this mystery.
In fact… Scripture confronts it directly.
And once you truly see it in its original language, context, and spiritual weight, Genesis will never feel like a children’s story again.
The world before Noah was not merely violent.
Something happened before the Flood so catastrophic that God Himself declared nearly all flesh ruined.
Because this was never merely about “big people.”
This was about rebellion against Heaven itself.
And the deeper you go, the more terrifying the implications become.
The Book of Genesis opens with haunting simplicity:
“When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them…” — Genesis 6:1
Then suddenly, Scripture says something that has shaken theologians, historians, and believers for thousands of years:
“The sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.” — Genesis 6:2
This exact phrase appears elsewhere in the Old Testament — especially in Job 1:6 and Job 2:1 — where it unmistakably refers to heavenly beings, angelic entities presenting themselves before God.
The oldest Hebrew understanding overwhelmingly recognized these as supernatural beings.
And the ancient Jewish world understood this passage with terrifying seriousness.
“The Nephilim were on the earth in those days…”

Or possibly:
“those who cause others to fall.”
And suddenly the Bible introduces a civilization most churches barely explain.
“These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.”
Scripture places them inside real human history.
And this is where things become chilling.
Because the Bible says the corruption became global.
“Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
But then Genesis 6:12 says something most readers overlook:
“All flesh had corrupted their way upon the earth.”
The Hebrew word for corrupted is:

Meaning:
to ruin,
to destroy,
to decay beyond repair.
Something had spread across creation itself.
And suddenly the Flood makes horrifying sense.
Because God was not simply judging bad behavior.

Ancient Jewish writings outside the canon — especially 1 Enoch — expand on this understanding in remarkable detail. While not Scripture itself, it reflects how many ancient Jews interpreted Genesis during the Second Temple period, including many ideas circulating during the time of Jesus.
1 Enoch describes rebellious angels called “Watchers” descending to earth under a leader named Shemihazah.
And their offspring became giants who devoured mankind.
The New Testament appears to reference this event directly.
“For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell…”
The Greek word for “hell” here is not Gehenna.
Peter continues by connecting this event directly to Noah and the Flood.
“And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling…”

“ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον”
(apolipontas to idion oikētērion)

Meaning:
they abandoned their proper habitation.
And Jude immediately compares this sin to sexual immorality.
“As the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” — Matthew 24:37
Most people think that only means wickedness.
But what if Jesus was warning about something deeper?
Humanity attempting to become godlike again.
The modern world suddenly feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because our generation is obsessed with forbidden knowledge.
The rejection of God’s created order.
And beneath all of it is the oldest temptation in history:
And maybe that is why this mystery grips people so deeply.
Because deep down, humanity remembers fragments of a shattered world.

Almost every ancient civilization carries legends of giant beings:
the Titans of Greece,
the Apkallu of Mesopotamia,
the Jotnar of Norse mythology,
the giant clans of Canaan.

Even after the Flood, Scripture records remnants of giant bloodlines:
the Anakim,
the Rephaim,
Og king of Bashan,
and of course…
The giant David faced was not mythology.
He was the shadow of an older horror.
But this story is not ultimately about giants.
It is about contamination versus redemption.
Because from Genesis onward, Satan’s war was always aimed at the promised Seed.
If corruption could destroy humanity completely, the prophecy of Genesis 3:15 could never be fulfilled.
But God preserved a bloodline through Noah.
God preserved humanity through judgment because redemption was still coming.
The true Son of God came to undo what the fallen sons corrupted.
And at the Cross, the kingdom of darkness suffered its ultimate defeat.
“He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame…”
Christ publicly humiliated the powers of darkness through His sacrifice.
That means the deepest terror of Genesis 6 does not end with fear.
Because no corruption is greater than His redemption.
No darkness is stronger than His blood.
No fallen kingdom can overpower the resurrected Christ.
And maybe someone reading this feels contaminated too.
The Gospel is the story of God rescuing corrupted people.
For people barely holding themselves together at 2AM.
For people pretending to smile while silently collapsing inside.
And maybe that’s why this ancient mystery hits so hard.
Because the real giants were never only outside humanity.
This hit deeper than a history lesson.
Some mysteries in the Bible were never meant to entertain you.
They were meant to warn you.
